about: The fifth answer choice for each bank question a practice exam uses (docs/apmacro-architecture.md, "Practice exams"). The exam has five choices, (A) to (E) (needs-author mcq-options); the practice bank keeps four. The generator serves each question in a form with its four options, then this one, and its explanation (why). Keys and explanations of the four stay in the bank.

mac-scarcity-10.option: Economic growth, because she finds more uses for her time
mac-scarcity-10.why: Growth would mean more time or resources; she still has three hours, so choosing among her wants is scarcity.

mac-opportunity-cost-ppc-17.option: It shifts out for consumer goods and in for capital goods
mac-opportunity-cost-ppc-17.why: More capital raises what the economy can make of both goods, so the curve shifts outward; no part of it moves in.

mac-comparative-advantage-13.option: The country with the absolute advantage gains, and the other loses
mac-comparative-advantage-13.why: Gains from trade come from different opportunity costs; with equal costs neither country gains, whoever has the absolute advantage.

mac-demand-14.option: Each extra unit costs sellers more to make
mac-demand-14.why: Rising cost per unit explains why supply slopes up; the demand curve is about buyers' choices at each price.

mac-supply-14.option: Sellers make more units at low prices to keep their revenue up
mac-supply-14.why: At a lower price, producing extra units is less worthwhile, so the quantity supplied falls; that is why supply slopes up.

mac-gdp-circular-flow-16.option: Profit is left out of both totals, so they match
mac-gdp-circular-flow-16.why: Profit is income to the owners of firms and is counted in the income total; it is part of why spending and income match.

mac-gdp-circular-flow-15.option: the GDP of whichever country collects her income tax
mac-gdp-circular-flow-15.why: GDP counts output produced inside a country's borders, whoever produces it; where her taxes go does not change that.

mac-gdp-limitations-16.option: One has a higher GDP per capita than the other
mac-gdp-limitations-16.why: The question says the two have the same GDP per capita, so this is not a difference between them.

mac-unemployment-16.option: She counts as a discouraged worker, so the rate is unaffected
mac-unemployment-16.why: A discouraged worker has no job and has stopped looking; Ivy has a job, so the survey counts her as employed.

mac-price-indices-inflation-13.why: The real wage changes by about the nominal change minus inflation: $3\% - 5\% = -2\%$, not the two added together.

mac-inflation-costs-15.option: The bank gains, because the houses it lent against are worth more
mac-inflation-costs-15.why: The loan is repaid in a fixed number of dollars; a higher house price does not raise what the bank is paid, so surprise inflation hurts the lender.

mac-real-nominal-gdp-16.option: It leaves out the prices of services
mac-real-nominal-gdp-16.why: The deflator covers every final good and service produced in the country, services included.

mac-business-cycles-19.option: A line that stays below real GDP in each year
mac-business-cycles-19.why: In contractions real GDP falls below potential, so potential output cannot sit below real GDP in every year.

mac-aggregate-demand-13.option: Its exports fall, because foreign buyers have less to spend
mac-aggregate-demand-13.why: Foreign incomes have not changed; a lower price level makes Country Z's goods cheaper abroad, so its exports rise.

mac-aggregate-demand-2.option: It shifts right, because net exports rose by 20
mac-aggregate-demand-2.why: Net exports did rise by 20, but investment fell by 50, so total planned spending at each price level fell by 30.

mac-multipliers-14.option: The firm's workers save the whole of their extra income
mac-multipliers-14.why: If every extra dollar were saved there would be no further rounds of spending, so total spending would rise by the first million alone.

mac-sras-5.option: A rise in the price level that lets firms charge more
mac-sras-5.why: A change in the price level is a movement along SRAS, not a shift of the curve.

mac-lras-16.option: Vertical at the price level where AD meets SRAS
mac-lras-16.why: LRAS stands at full-employment real GDP on the horizontal axis; it is not placed at a price level.

mac-adas-equilibrium-12.option: A recessionary gap of 50 billion dollars, with unemployment below the natural rate
mac-adas-equilibrium-12.why: Output above LRAS is an inflationary gap, not a recessionary one; unemployment is below the natural rate there.

mac-adas-short-run-changes-14.option: AD shifts left: the price level rises and real GDP falls
mac-adas-short-run-changes-14.why: A leftward AD shift lowers both the price level and real GDP; a higher price level with lower output comes from SRAS shifting left.

mac-long-run-self-adjustment-14.option: The original price level with real GDP back at full employment
mac-long-run-self-adjustment-14.why: Nominal wages rise and SRAS shifts left, so output returns to full employment at a higher price level, not the old one.

mac-fiscal-policy-14.option: The spending is counted in GDP once the bill passes, not when it is spent
mac-fiscal-policy-14.why: GDP counts spending when the goods and services are produced; the problem is timing, since the money may arrive after the gap has closed.

mac-automatic-stabilizers-15.option: Tax collections rise in the downturn, so AD shifts right
mac-automatic-stabilizers-15.why: A fixed tax per household does not change with income, so collections stay the same in a downturn; nothing pushes AD right.

mac-financial-assets-12.option: Creating new money to pay for the factory
mac-financial-assets-12.why: Only the central bank creates money this way; a company that sells bonds is borrowing from the people who buy them.

mac-financial-assets-18.why: A bond can be sold quickly in the bond market, so it is more liquid than a house, which takes weeks and fees to sell.

mac-nominal-real-rates-15.option: The real rate is the same as the nominal rate
mac-nominal-real-rates-15.why: The two differ by expected inflation; they are equal when expected inflation is zero, which is not the general case.

mac-nominal-real-rates-8.option: A fixed nominal rate agreed before the surprise
mac-nominal-real-rates-8.why: A fixed nominal rate is what left the bank exposed: when inflation came in above what was expected, the real rate it earned fell.

mac-money-functions-10.option: The difficulty of saving for the future
mac-money-functions-10.why: Saving is about money as a store of value; the plumber's problem is trading today, which money as a medium of exchange solves.

mac-money-functions-15.option: The bank deposits that back each bill
mac-money-functions-15.why: Fiat money is backed by no commodity or deposit; its value rests on government decree and people's willingness to accept it.

mac-banking-money-supply-14.why: Required reserves fall by \$100, but reserves fall by the full \$1,000, so excess reserves fall by $1{,}000 - 100 = 900$ dollars.

mac-money-market-14.option: The central bank raises the money supply until the rate matches
mac-money-market-14.why: The market moves back by itself: people buy bonds with the money they do not want to hold, bond prices rise and the rate falls.

mac-monetary-policy-18.option: The money supply falls and interest rates fall
mac-monetary-policy-18.why: A lower discount rate makes borrowing reserves cheaper, so banks lend more and the money supply rises, not falls.

mac-loanable-funds-17.option: A higher real interest rate makes borrowers want more funds
mac-loanable-funds-17.why: Borrowers want fewer funds at a higher rate, which is why demand slopes down; supply slopes up because savers lend more.

mac-policy-short-run-15.option: Both shift SRAS; fiscal policy through taxes, monetary policy through wages
mac-policy-short-run-15.why: In the short run both work on demand: spending, taxes and interest rates change AD, not SRAS.

mac-policy-short-run-12.why: Both actions in Bela are expansionary, so AD rises for sure; the interest rate is the variable the two push in opposite directions.

mac-phillips-curve-17.option: The economy moves down along the SRPC: inflation falls and unemployment rises
mac-phillips-curve-17.why: A movement along the SRPC comes from a change in AD; a supply shock shifts the SRPC itself, here to the left.

mac-phillips-curve-15.option: In the long run, inflation and unemployment rise and fall together
mac-phillips-curve-15.why: The vertical LRPC says unemployment is at the natural rate whatever inflation is: no long-run link at all, not a positive one.

mac-money-growth-inflation-13.option: In the long run, the money supply returns to its old level by itself
mac-money-growth-inflation-13.why: Nothing removes the new money; output returns to full employment because wages and prices adjust up, leaving a higher price level.

mac-money-growth-inflation-7.option: They fall, because loans will be repaid in more valuable money
mac-money-growth-inflation-7.why: High expected inflation means money will be worth less when loans are repaid, so lenders raise nominal rates.

mac-deficits-debt-12.option: It shrinks, because higher rates cut spending on programs
mac-deficits-debt-12.why: The question holds programs unchanged; higher rates raise interest outlays, so the deficit grows.

mac-crowding-out-15.option: When firms have many profitable projects and the government borrows nothing
mac-crowding-out-15.why: Crowding out comes from government borrowing; with no new borrowing there is nothing to crowd private investment out.

mac-economic-growth-14.option: Productivity matters mainly in recessions, when it raises AD
mac-economic-growth-14.why: Productivity raises output per worker and LRAS year after year; it is a long-run supply story, not a recession fix.

mac-growth-policy-15.option: The money supply rises, so the real interest rate falls
mac-growth-policy-15.why: Transfers are fiscal policy and do not change the money supply; their main effect is on consumption and AD.

mac-balance-of-payments-14.option: Its current account balance rises, because fewer goods leave the country
mac-balance-of-payments-14.why: Exports are a credit in the current account, so fewer exports lower the current account balance.

mac-exchange-rates-15.option: Student A, while Student B describes a different change
mac-exchange-rates-15.why: Both students describe the same move from its two sides: when the arl buys more bels, each bel buys fewer arls.

mac-foreign-exchange-market-15.option: Demand for arls falls, and supply of bels falls
mac-foreign-exchange-market-15.why: Arland buyers need bels to pay Belvian sellers, so they supply arls and demand bels; neither of these falls.

mac-fx-policy-changes-15.option: It appreciates, because the money supply in Arland rises
mac-fx-policy-changes-15.why: More money and lower Arland interest rates make Arland assets less attractive, so demand for arls falls and the arl depreciates.

mac-fx-net-exports-15.option: An Arland family planning a holiday in Belvia
mac-fx-net-exports-15.why: A stronger arl buys more bels, so a holiday in Belvia gets cheaper for the family; they gain from the appreciation.

mac-real-rates-financial-flows-16.option: Into Arland, because its real interest rate is higher
mac-real-rates-financial-flows-16.why: Arland's real rate is $7\% - 4\% = 3\%$ and Belvia's is $5\% - 1\% = 4\%$, so Belvia's real rate is the higher one.

mac-scarcity-11.why: Growth would raise what the city can do in total; here a fixed budget went to one use and another was given up, a trade-off.

mac-opportunity-cost-ppc-18.option: The economy produces at a point inside the curve
mac-opportunity-cost-ppc-18.why: A point inside the curve means unused resources; it says nothing about why the curve itself is bowed.

mac-demand-15.why: Coffee and tea are substitutes: a rise in the price of one raises the demand for the other. Complements are used together.

mac-supply-9.option: Demand for honey decreases this month
mac-supply-9.why: The makers' expectations shift supply; and buyers who expect a higher price would buy more now, not less.

mac-market-equilibrium-10.why: At \$1 the new quantity demanded is 120 cups and the quantity supplied 30, a shortage, not an equilibrium.

mac-gdp-circular-flow-14.option: As exports, because they leave the factory
mac-gdp-circular-flow-14.why: Exports are sales to buyers abroad; chairs made this year and not yet sold are counted as investment in inventory.

mac-gdp-limitations-15.option: GDP leaves out the value of used goods sold this year
mac-gdp-limitations-15.why: Used goods are left out of GDP, but that is not this example; here the price stays the same while the phone does far more.

mac-unemployment-17.option: It stays the same, because new graduates are counted once they are hired
mac-unemployment-17.why: People without a job who are looking for one count as unemployed from the start, so the rate rises at once.

mac-price-indices-inflation-15.option: The cost of the basket in that year
mac-price-indices-inflation-15.why: The index divides the basket's cost by its own base-year cost and multiplies by 100, so it is 100, not a dollar amount.

mac-inflation-costs-16.option: Inflation lowers the price of the machines the factory needs
mac-inflation-costs-16.why: Inflation is a rise in the general price level; the planning problem is that future costs and prices are hard to predict.

mac-inflation-costs-14.option: Interest on a savings account whose rate is reset with inflation
mac-inflation-costs-14.why: A rate reset with inflation keeps up with prices, so this income is not fixed in dollars.

mac-real-nominal-gdp-14.option: Real GDP is zero, because no inflation has happened yet
mac-real-nominal-gdp-14.why: In the base year real GDP is output valued at base-year prices, which are that year's prices, so it equals nominal GDP.

mac-business-cycles-10.option: By importing more goods than it exports
mac-business-cycles-10.why: Imports are produced abroad and do not add to Berovia's output; producing above potential comes from using resources harder for a while.

mac-aggregate-demand-17.option: SRAS shifts right, because workers keep more of their pay
mac-aggregate-demand-17.why: The tax cut raises disposable income and consumption, which shifts AD; SRAS depends on firms' costs of production.

mac-multipliers-9.option: The MPS equals 1 divided by the MPC
mac-multipliers-9.why: The MPC and MPS add up to 1, so the MPS is $1 - \text{MPC}$; 1 divided by the MPS is the spending multiplier.

mac-sras-16.why: Rules that raise the cost of each unit lower what firms supply at each price level; they shift SRAS left and add no capacity.

mac-lras-4.option: It would shift inward, because the population grew
mac-lras-4.why: More labor and capital raise what the economy can produce, so the curve shifts outward, not inward.

mac-adas-equilibrium-16.option: On the vertical axis where AD meets LRAS
mac-adas-equilibrium-16.why: YF is a level of real GDP, so it goes on the horizontal axis where LRAS stands, not on the price level axis.

mac-adas-short-run-changes-4.option: AD shifted right: the price level and real GDP both rose
mac-adas-short-run-changes-4.why: From Year 3 to Year 4 the price level fell from 110 to 108 and real GDP from 820 to 790, so AD shifted left.

mac-adas-short-run-changes-8.option: It falls at first, then returns to its old level
mac-adas-short-run-changes-8.why: Higher fuel costs shift SRAS left and the foreign boom shifts AD right; both push the price level up at once.

mac-long-run-self-adjustment-13.option: It names AD; the mechanism is LRAS shifting right
mac-long-run-self-adjustment-13.why: LRAS stays where it is; the economy returns to it because falling nominal wages shift SRAS right.

mac-long-run-self-adjustment-15.option: The government raises spending to shift AD right
mac-long-run-self-adjustment-15.why: The question says no policy is used; lower wages and input prices shift SRAS back right on their own.

mac-fiscal-policy-15.option: It is lower, because the gap closes sooner
mac-fiscal-policy-15.why: Closing the gap sooner does not lower prices; spending shifts AD right, so the price level ends higher than with self-adjustment.

mac-automatic-stabilizers-11.option: The central bank decides when they start
mac-automatic-stabilizers-11.why: Automatic stabilizers are parts of the tax and transfer system; they act without a new decision by the central bank or the legislature.

mac-financial-assets-13.option: It is the share of a deposit a bank keeps as reserves
mac-financial-assets-13.why: That describes a reserve ratio; an interest rate is the yearly cost of borrowing, as a percent of the loan.

mac-nominal-real-rates-4.option: The lender expects inflation of zero
mac-nominal-real-rates-4.why: Loan D's lender expects inflation of 5%; the real rate is $5\% - 5\% = 0$, which means no gain in buying power.

mac-money-functions-13.option: It rises by \$2,000 as the bank lends
mac-money-functions-13.why: Right away, \$200 of cash in M1 becomes \$200 of checkable deposits in M1, so M1 is unchanged; any lending comes later.

mac-banking-money-supply-11.why: With a ratio of 0.1 the money multiplier is $\frac{1}{0.1} = 10$, and with 0.2 it is $\frac{1}{0.2} = 5$.

mac-money-market-18.option: Money demand is vertical, so money supply is drawn the same way
mac-money-market-18.why: Money demand slopes down; the money supply is vertical because the central bank sets its quantity.

mac-money-market-13.why: The vertical axis is the nominal interest rate, the opportunity cost of holding money instead of bonds.

mac-monetary-policy-21.option: Printing currency to pay for government spending
mac-monetary-policy-21.why: With ample reserves the central bank moves the policy rate with its administered rates; paying for government spending is not a monetary policy tool.

mac-monetary-policy-4.option: Neither gap; aggregate demand does not change
mac-monetary-policy-4.why: The graph shows a change in the policy rate, and a change in interest rates shifts AD in the short run.

mac-loanable-funds-8.option: National saving falls to 300 and the real rate falls
mac-loanable-funds-8.why: National saving is now $400 - 100 = 300$; balancing the budget raises it to 400, so it rises, and the real rate falls.

mac-loanable-funds-4.option: It rises, because the supply of loanable funds shifted right
mac-loanable-funds-4.why: The supply curve did not move; demand shifted right, the real rate rose, and savers lent more along the supply curve.

mac-policy-short-run-4.option: AD is unchanged; the interest rate falls for sure
mac-policy-short-run-4.why: Both policies are expansionary, so AD rises by more than with either one alone.

mac-phillips-curve-18.why: The PPC is not part of the AD-AS model; the LRPC matches LRAS, both vertical at full employment.

mac-money-growth-inflation-10.option: The share of extra income that people save
mac-money-growth-inflation-10.why: That is the MPS; velocity is how many times a year the average dollar is spent on final output.

mac-deficits-debt-10.option: A surplus appears, because output rises
mac-deficits-debt-10.why: Lower taxes and more spending widen the deficit; a recovery may offset part of it, not turn it into a surplus.

mac-crowding-out-13.option: A rise in private investment when government spending raises demand
mac-crowding-out-13.why: That is the opposite effect; crowding out is a fall in private investment as government borrowing raises the real rate.

mac-crowding-out-8.option: A fall in the real interest rate caused by more government borrowing
mac-crowding-out-8.why: More government borrowing raises the real interest rate, which is what crowds out investment; it does not lower it.

mac-economic-growth-12.why: Financial capital is money raised to invest; the nurse's new skill is human capital, the knowledge and skill of workers.

mac-economic-growth-5.option: Alton's nominal GDP rose faster than Breck's
mac-economic-growth-5.why: Both raised real GDP by 10 percent; per capita growth depends on population, and Breck's grew as fast as its output.

mac-growth-policy-13.why: Patents reward invention, which is new technology; physical capital is machines, tools and buildings.

mac-growth-policy-9.option: Lowering interest rates to raise investment
mac-growth-policy-9.why: That is monetary policy; supply-side fiscal policy uses taxes and spending to raise incentives and shift LRAS right.

mac-balance-of-payments-12.option: As a credit in the capital and financial account
mac-balance-of-payments-12.why: Interest paid abroad is income leaving the country, a debit in the current account; it is not a sale of a financial asset.

mac-exchange-rates-13.option: The rate moves from 4 bels per arl to 2 bels per arl
mac-exchange-rates-13.why: Fewer bels per arl means each bel costs more arls, so the tuition fixed in bels costs the student more.

mac-foreign-exchange-market-14.option: When the arl is cheaper, Belvians earn more bels
mac-foreign-exchange-market-14.why: Belvian incomes in bels do not change with the price of the arl; Arland goods cost fewer bels, so Belvians want more arls.

mac-fx-policy-changes-16.option: Supply of bels falls next month, so nothing changes now
mac-fx-policy-changes-16.why: Expectations act now: traders buy bels today to gain from the expected rise, so demand for bels rises and the bel appreciates now.

mac-fx-net-exports-4.option: They rose by twice the amount Arland's fell
mac-fx-net-exports-4.why: With two countries trading with each other alone, one's net exports are the other's net imports, so Belvia's rose by exactly what Arland's fell.

mac-real-rates-financial-flows-18.option: The real rate rises by more, because the arl appreciates
mac-real-rates-financial-flows-18.why: The appreciation follows the inflow; the inflow itself adds to the supply of loanable funds, so the real rate rises by less.
